questions.question: What does $f_n\rightrightarrows f$ on $X$ mean?
options: For every $x\in X$, there is an $N$ depending on $x$ such that $|f_n(x)-f(x)| \lt \varepsilon$.
The functions $f_n$ are all equal to $f$ after some fixed $N$.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there is an $N$ such that for all $n \gt N$ and all $x\in X$, $|f_n(x)-f(x)| \lt \varepsilon$.
The values $f_n(x)$ are increasing for every $x\in X$.
questions.explanation: $f_n\rightrightarrows f$ on $X$ means: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ (independent of $x$) such that for all $n>N$ and all $x\in X$, $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$.
questions.source_support: This is the definition of uniform convergence on the concept.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: An $N$ depending on $x$ gives pointwise convergence, not uniform; uniform convergence requires a single $N$ working for every $x\in X$.
The $f_n$ need not equal $f$ exactly after any $N$; they need only satisfy $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$, e.g. $f_n(x)=x/n\rightrightarrows 0$ without ever equaling $0$.
Uniform convergence does not require monotonicity; the definition bounds $|f_n-f|$, with no condition on whether $f_n(x)$ increases or decreases.
